findings.issue_text: [BUG] The new cleanup path logs routine per-batch diagnostics via r.log.Error at Error level, including the full fetched ID slice and an always-nil "err" field. Every annotation cleanup cycle emits error-level log lines with up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize IDs each (e.g. 32767 IDs) for both the MaxAge and MaxCount passes; with the ticker now at 1 minute (cleanup.go), operators get error-log flooding and false error alerts on every healthy run.

[BUG] The MaxCount cleanup branch repeats the same r.log.Error debug logging with the full ID array and a nil err per batch. Same error-level log flooding as the MaxAge branch, repeated each batch and each minute; monitoring keyed on error-level logs from the cleanup service fires constantly on healthy systems.

[BUG] CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags also uses r.log.Error for informational per-batch output including the full orphaned-tag ID list and a nil "err" value. Orphaned-tag cleanup, which now runs every minute, emits error-level spam listing up to batch-size IDs per batch; on instances with many orphaned tags this floods logs and pages on-call via any error-log alerting.

[ADVISORY] The cleanup ticker is hardcoded from 10 minutes to 1 minute with no configuration flag or feature gate, a 10x frequency increase for every consumer of CleanUpService. Operators of large Grafana instances now run annotation cleanup (which does a full-table ID fetch per configured cleanup setting) every minute with no way to tune or disable the interval without a code deploy; combined with the error-level logging above, log volume and DB query load increase 10x immediately on upgrade.

[ADVISORY] The new SQLite-variable-limit test case (40003 annotations, batch size 32767) makes the previously fast unit test insert and delete ~40k rows plus ~80k tag rows, and the test is guarded only by testing.Short(), not an integration build tag despite the TestIntegration rename. Renaming to TestIntegration* without an actual build-tag guard (only testing.Short) means CI runs that don't pass -short still execute this heavy case inline with the other cases, significantly slowing the package's test cycle and masking the intended integration-test separation.

[BUG] The new batched cleanup logs at Error level on every successful batch, dumping the full fetched ID slice into the log (e.g. `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err)` at xorm_store.go:529 and the identical pattern at lines 533, 552, 556, and 563), where `err` is also always nil at those call sites. On a real Grafana instance with millions of annotations, a single cleanup run emits thousands of Error-level log lines, each potentially containing up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize (default large) IDs, flooding logs and pager/alerting on error-level output during normal operation; operators see thousands of "errors" for a routine job and the nil "err" field is dead weight.

[ADVISORY] The cleanup ticker interval change from 10 minutes to 1 minute (`ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)`) is shipped with no verification and no documentation of the intended interval, and it applies to every job the CleanUpService runs, not just annotation cleanup. Operators who tuned load expectations around a 10-minute sweep (including the old single-statement annotation cleanup) now see a 10x increase in cleanup-job database activity; the next maintainer cannot tell whether the 1-minute value is a leftover debugging setting from this PR or intentional, and the diff's own test suite never asserts or documents the interval.

[ADVISORY] deleteByIDs has a dialect/limit matrix (SQLite + batch size > 999 → string-interpolated IDs; otherwise → placeholders) but the test matrix only exercises the interpolation path (SQLite test with batch size 32767) and the tiny placeholder path (batch size 1); no test covers the placeholder path with more than 999 IDs on SQLite, i.e. batch sizes of exactly 999 or 1000 where the branch boundary lives. A future change to the `sqliteParameterLimit` constant or the boundary comparison (`>` vs `>=`) passes the existing tests while breaking real SQLite deployments at batch size exactly 999/1000 with 'too many SQL variables' errors; the boundary condition that the SQLite test name claims to verify is not actually pinned.

[ADVISORY] CleanAnnotations' MaxCount branch loops via untilDoneOrCancelled, but unlike the MaxAge branch the code comment does not note that the code claims "any such annotations will simply be cleaned on the next cycle" — the under-delete-on-concurrent-inserts caveat documented for the MaxAge path applies equally here, and more importantly the loop condition (stop when a batch affects zero rows) is now coupled to deleteByIDs's RowsAffected rather than the fetched ID count, so a batch that fetches IDs but deletes 0 rows (e.g. rows already deleted by a concurrent process) silently terminates the loop even though the condition still matches more rows. With two cleanup instances (or a concurrent manual cleanup) racing, the loser fetches IDs, deletes 0, and stops early — the affected-rows-as-termination-signal conflation turns a transient race into a permanently skipped remainder until the next run, with no test in the diff covering partial/zero-affected termination.

[BUG] The MaxAge cleanup path logs normal-operation progress at Error level via r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ...), including the full fetched ID slice and a guaranteed-nil err. Every successful cleanup batch emits an ERROR-level log with up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize (e.g. 32767) IDs serialized into it, flooding logs, breaking alerting on real errors, and the nil "err" field misleads operators into thinking failures occurred; this also partially negates the performance goal of the PR on large deployments.

[BUG] The MaxCount cleanup path logs normal-operation progress at Error level with the full ID slice and a nil err. Same log-flood and false-error-alarm failure mode as the MaxAge site; every batch of the count-based cleanup is reported as an error to operators.

[BUG] CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags logs normal-operation progress at Error level with the full ID slice and a nil err. Orphaned-tag cleanup batches are logged as errors with thousands of IDs per batch, polluting error dashboards and masking genuine failures.

[ADVISORY] The cleanup job ticker interval is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute with no accompanying requirement, config option, or PR-scope justification ("Database Performance Optimizations"). Every Grafana instance runs the annotation cleanup DB workload 10x more often after this PR, a hot-path regression for DB load that operators cannot tune without a code deploy, and the change is not traceable to any stated requirement in the PR intent.

[ADVISORY] deleteByIDs special-cases SQLite's 999-parameter limit with inline ID interpolation but leaves every other dialect on placeholder expansion, so a configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above MySQL's ~65535 prepared-statement parameter limit produces a failing DELETE per batch. An operator who raises the batch size on MySQL past 65535 gets a hard error on every cleanup cycle (cleanup job stops making progress for that rule), with no clamp or validation of the setting anywhere in the diff.

[ADVISORY] t.Cleanup for the annotation/annotation_tag tables is registered only after createTestAnnotations succeeds, and the shared fakeSQL is reused across subtests, so any partial failure during the new 40003-row InsertMulti leaves rows that leak into the subsequent subtests' assertAnnotationCount. A mid-creation failure in one subtest (now far more likely with the new 40003-row case) corrupts the counts asserted by later subtests, producing confusing cross-test failures instead of an isolated failure.

[ADVISORY] Routine success-path cleanup logging is emitted at Error level, including the full ID slice and the condition string, via r.log.Error. Every annotation cleanup cycle floods operator error logs/alerting with 'Annotations to clean by time'/'cleaned annotations by count'/'cleaned tags' Error entries on perfectly healthy runs; on a large install with the 1-minute ticker this is thousands of bogus error lines per hour, masking real errors.

[ADVISORY] The MaxCount branch logs at r.log.Error and also passes the already-handled err variable again as a log field after the if err != nil early return inside the closure. Error-level noise for normal batches (same as the MaxAge site), plus the 'err' field is always nil at this point, training whoever greps logs to distrust these entries.

[ADVISORY] CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags uses r.log.Error with the orphan tag ID list for every batch on the success path. Operators see persistent Error-severity log lines naming deleted tag IDs on every healthy cleanup cycle, polluting error dashboards and potentially writing very large log lines when a batch has thousands of IDs.

[ADVISORY] The SQLite inline-values branch builds the IN list with repeated fmt.Sprintf concatenation (values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)), which is O(n^2) in the number of IDs in the batch. With a large AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize (the code explicitly supports batches like 32767+, and the added test creates 40003), the string is reallocated ~n times producing ~800M bytes of copying per batch on the SQLite path; a string.Builder/strings.Join makes this linear — the next editor tuning batch size gets a silent quadratic blowup in the cleanup job.

[ADVISORY] The cleanup ticker interval is silently changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute in a PR labeled 'Database Performance Optimizations', with no config knob or migration note. Every Grafana instance now runs the full cleanup job (tmp-file sweep plus all annotation cleanup queries, including the new SELECT-id batches) 10x as often; deployments with large annotation tables where cleanup finds nothing still pay the query cost every minute, and operators who relied on the documented 10-minute cadence see a 10x increase in background DB load with no way to configure it back without a code change.

[BUG] Debug leftover calls use r.log.Error to emit per-batch progress messages ('Annotations to clean by time', 'cleaned annotations by time', etc.) at error level on every cleanup cycle. Every Grafana instance's logs fill with ERROR-level lines (including full ID lists up to batch size) from routine successful cleanup runs; operators monitoring error-level logs get spurious alerts and the real error signal is drowned, defeating the logging intent of this service.

[BUG] The MaxCount cleanup and orphaned-tag cleanup reuse the same r.log.Error debug pattern, logging the entire fetched ID slice at error level on every batch. With AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize in the thousands, each batch emits thousands of IDs at ERROR level, producing multi-megabyte log lines per cleanup run and corrupting the log contract that errors indicate failures.

[ADVISORY] The rewritten MaxAge path changes deletion semantics from a single atomic DELETE to fetch-then-delete, which under-deletes when concurrent inserts occur between fetch and delete. The comment acknowledges this drift; the visible contract of Run's returned affectedAnnotations count and per-cycle cleanup guarantees silently weaken versus the prior behavior — next reviewer should confirm this trade-off was accepted, not slipped in during review iteration.

[ADVISORY] The MaxCount branch still uses fetchIDs with LimitOffset(batchSize, MaxCount) inside untilDoneOrCancelled, so each iteration deletes a batch of IDs that lie beyond the keep-count, meaning the callback can loop indefinitely re-selecting overlapping ranges if deletes don't shrink the qualifying set. If a batch's delete affects fewer rows than fetched (e.g., concurrent row re-creation or the under-delete path), the loop re-fetches the same offset window and can spin without progressing until context cancellation; the original single-statement loop's exit condition (zero affected rows) no longer maps cleanly to 'done' here.

[ADVISORY] The cleanup job ticker interval silently changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute as part of a PR titled 'Database Performance Optimizations', with no config option and no mention in the change. Every deployment now runs annotation cleanup queries 10x more often, a behavior-frequency change unrelated to the stated intent; operators relying on the documented 10-minute cadence get surprise DB load, and this intent drift was not surfaced for acceptance.

[ADVISORY] Debug/diagnostic logging is emitted at Error level on every cleanup batch, including a full list of deleted annotation IDs and a hardcoded nil "err" key (r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err) and the three sibling sites at ~lines 550, 562, and 573). Operators running annotation cleanup on a large install get every batch logged at ERROR severity with thousands of integer IDs and raw SQL condition strings, flooding logs/alerting and drowning genuine errors; the always-present "err" key logs a nil error, so error-rate alerting keyed on log level fires on every successful run.

[ADVISORY] Renaming TestAnnotationCleanUp and TestOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst to TestIntegration* with a testing.Short() skip removes all coverage of the completely rewritten CleanAnnotations/CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags delete strategy from any -short test invocation. The rewritten fetch-IDs-then-delete batching logic in this same diff (xorm_store.go) gets zero test coverage in short-mode CI runs; a regression in batched deletion ships undetected to production databases.

[BUG] The new batching code logs routine informational messages ('Annotations to clean by time', 'cleaned annotations by count', 'Tags to clean', 'cleaned tags') at Error level via r.log.Error, including an 'err' key that is provably nil at those call sites. Every successful cleanup cycle (now running every minute per the cleanup.go ticker change) emits error-level log lines with nil errors containing full ID lists, spamming operator alerting and making real errors indistinguishable from normal operation; no test asserts log levels so this passes silently.

[ADVISORY] The new error and lifecycle branches — fetchIDs' empty-condition error return, untilDoneOrCancelled's ctx.Done() cancellation path, and deleteByIDs' len(ids)==0 early return — are exercised by no test in the diff (checked cleanup_test.go, the only test file changed; all four subtests run the happy path with a live context and non-empty result sets). The context-cancellation path that returns partial totalAffected plus ctx.Err(), central to the job being safely cancellable at shutdown, has no regression protection; a future refactor that drops the select-on-ctx check (reintroducing the old unbounded loop) passes the entire suite.

[ADVISORY] createTestAnnotations now inserts 500 annotations per InsertMulti call (~7500+ bound parameters per statement), which only works because modern SQLite (>= 3.32.0) raised SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER to 32766 — the exact limit the new 40003-row test case is nominally probing. On an environment with SQLite < 3.32.0 (999-parameter limit) the test fixture itself fails with 'too many SQL variables' before the cleanup logic under test is ever reached, producing a confusing fixture failure rather than a meaningful signal; the test's own name acknowledges the version dependency but the insert path does not guard against it.

[ADVISORY] The diff's stated reason for the rewrite — avoiding MySQL deadlocks with concurrent inserts, accepting under-deletion until the next cycle — is a behavioral property with no test anywhere in the diff (no concurrency test, no MySQL-backend test; all subtests run single-threaded against SQLite). The only observable behavioral difference the rewrite was made for (lock-flush behavior and under-deletion under concurrent writes) is unverified, so a refactor that reintroduces single-statement deletes on MySQL passes the full suite while regressing the production deadlock the change exists to fix.

[ADVISORY] Routine batch progress is logged at Error level, including the full ID slice, so every cleanup cycle emits multiple error-level lines with up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize (default potentially thousands) IDs each. Operators with error-level log alerting get paged every cycle by successful cleanup runs; with the ticker now firing every 1 minute (cleanup.go), a 32767-batch run can dump tens of thousands of IDs into logs each minute, bloating log storage and drowning real errors. Use Debug/Info and omit the id list.

[ADVISORY] The 'Annotations to clean' log statements pass an always-nil err (the code returns early on error before logging), and the paired post-delete log uses named returns x, y in an unidiomatic way, so log consumers see 'err=null' fields that look like a failed query result. Anyone grepping logs for 'err' on these Error-level lines misreads successful batches as failures; the nil err field is dead data that misleads incident triage.

[ADVISORY] The SQLite >999-parameters workaround is keyed on r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize rather than on len(ids), and other backends have parameter limits too (PostgreSQL caps at 65535), so a batch size configured above those limits still builds one giant placeholder list on non-SQLite databases. An operator on PostgreSQL who raises AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above 65535 (the config allows it) gets 'number of parameters must be between 0 and 65535' errors every cleanup cycle, deleting nothing; chunking the placeholder list in deleteByIDs regardless of dialect removes the per-backend limit knowledge.

[BUG] Cleanup success paths are logged at Error level with a nil err field ('r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ... "err", err)' and 'r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by time", ...)', repeated identically in the MaxCount block and in CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags). Every successful batch emits Error-level log lines containing an "err": null key, so operators running error-based alerting on Grafana's logs see a flood of spurious 'errors' from this background job on every cleanup run; the debug strings are clearly intended as temporary logging left in the shipped code.

[ADVISORY] The 'Annotations to clean by time' Error log includes the full ids slice, which is bounded by AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize and reaches tens of thousands of entries (the new test uses 32767). Operators with a large configured batch size get multi-hundred-kilobyte log lines per batch per minute (the ticker was also reduced from 10 minutes to 1), inflating log storage and making log streams unusable for the 40000-annotation case the PR itself targets.

[ADVISORY] The SQL-parameter-limit workaround is special-cased to SQLite (migrator.SQLite && batch size > 999), leaving other dialects' placeholder limits unhandled — e.g. SQL Server's 2100-parameter cap. An operator on SQL Server who sets AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above 2100 gets a driver error on every DELETE batch, so the cleanup job fails permanently on every run; the IDs-into-SQL fallback should be keyed on the dialect's actual parameter limit rather than a SQLite-only branch.

[ADVISORY] The cleanup ticker interval was shortened from 10 minutes to 1 minute with no accompanying config knob. Every Grafana instance now runs the annotation cleanup query path (multiple SELECT + DELETE batches plus orphan-tag sweeps) 10x more often, a hot-path load increase on the annotation table for all deployments, bundled in a PR whose stated goal is performance; operators cannot revert to the old cadence without a code change.

[ADVISORY] The batch loop terminates on 'affected == 0' rather than on 'no IDs fetched', so when a fetched ID is concurrently deleted before the DELETE runs (race acknowledged in the comment), deleteByIDs returns affected < len(ids), and if an entire batch races the loop exits early having deleted only part of the eligible set while untilDoneOrCancelled reports success. A cleanup run silently under-deletes and returns nil error with a partial total; the comment says the next cycle compensates, but with the loop exiting on affected==0 the run's returned affectedAnnotations count understates the work, which the cleanup service records as the run's result.

goldens.comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.

The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.

adjudication.rationale: In `xorm_store.go`, the new cleanup loops for both MaxAge and MaxCount unconditionally call `r.log.Error(...)` on the healthy path, including logging the full `ids` slice and an `err` variable that is typically `nil` after the prior `if err != nil` check (e.g., `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by count", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err)`). adjudication.rationale: In `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags`, the new per-batch logging uses `r.log.Error(...)` for normal control flow, including dumping the full `ids` slice and logging an `err` field that will commonly be `nil` (see the added `r.log.Error("Tags to clean", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err)` and `r.log.Error("cleaned tags", ...)` blocks). This is verifiably error-level spam and can trigger error-log alerting. The diff also changes a service ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute (`cleanup.go`), increasing the potential frequency of such spam, though the direct call path to orphaned-tag cleanup isn't shown in this diff.

The only guard is `if testing.Short() { t.Skip(...) }`; there is no build-tag separation in the file. Renaming the test to `TestIntegration*` does not change execution behavior for `go test`, so on CI runs that don’t pass `-short`, this heavy case will run as part of normal package tests and can significantly slow the suite. This is a concrete diff-grounded operational/performance concern (log flooding / misleading error-level logs), but it doesn’t by itself break cleanup correctness, so it’s not a functional defect.

adjudication.rationale: The diff explicitly changes the global cleanup loop interval in `pkg/services/cleanup/cleanup.go` from `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` to `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)`, which affects the entire `CleanUpService.Run` cadence (not annotation-only). adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] deleteByIDs has a dialect/limit matrix (SQLite + batch size > 999 → string-interpolated IDs; otherwise → placeholders) but the test matrix only exercises the interpolation path (SQLite test with batch size 32767) and the tiny placeholder path (batch size 1); no test covers the placeholder path with more than 999 IDs on SQLite, i.e. batch sizes of exactly 999 or 1000 where the branch boundary lives. adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new SQLite-specific branch in `deleteByIDs`: for SQLite, it switches from placeholders to string-interpolated IDs when `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999` (see `sqliteParameterLimit` and the `if r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` block). The updated test matrix only exercises batch size `1` (placeholder path with 1 var) and `32767` (SQLite interpolation path). There is no test that pins the branch boundary behavior at exactly `999` vs `1000`, so an accidental change to the constant or the comparison (`>` vs `>=`) could pass current tests while regressing SQLite at the limit. (Note: the finding’s claim about “placeholder path with more than 999 IDs on SQLite” is not directly reachable here because `fetchIDs` uses `LIMIT batchSize`, but the boundary-coverage concern is still valid and diff-grounded.)

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] CleanAnnotations' MaxCount branch loops via untilDoneOrCancelled, but unlike the MaxAge branch the code comment does not note that the code claims "any such annotations will simply be cleaned on the next cycle" — the under-delete-on-concurrent-inserts caveat documented for the MaxAge path applies equally here, and more importantly the loop condition (stop when a batch affects zero rows) is now coupled to deleteByIDs's RowsAffected rather than the fetched ID count, so a batch that fetches IDs but deletes 0 rows (e.g. rows already deleted by a concurrent process) silently terminates the loop even though the condition still matches more rows. With two cleanup instances (or a concurrent manual cleanup) racing, the loser fetches IDs, deletes 0, and stops early — the affected-rows-as-termination-signal conflation turns a transient race into a permanently skipped remainder until the next run, with no test in the diff covering partial/zero-affected termination.

adjudication.rationale: In xorm_store.go, both MaxAge and MaxCount now use untilDoneOrCancelled with a batchWork callback that (1) fetches IDs via fetchIDs in one DB session, then (2) deletes via deleteByIDs in another session. untilDoneOrCancelled terminates when the callback returns 0 affected rows. Because there is now a race window between fetching IDs and deleting them, a concurrent cleanup (or other deleter) can delete the fetched IDs first, causing deleteByIDs to return RowsAffected==0 even though more rows still match the condition (i.e., there are further batches to process). That will prematurely stop the loop for this run. This premature-termination risk is introduced/enabled by the new two-step fetch+delete approach and is not mitigated by using len(ids) as the continuation signal, nor is it tested in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The MaxAge cleanup path logs normal-operation progress at Error level via r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ...), including the full fetched ID slice and a guaranteed-nil err. Every successful cleanup batch emits an ERROR-level log with up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize (e.g. 32767) IDs serialized into it, flooding logs, breaking alerting on real errors, and the nil "err" field misleads operators into thinking failures occurred; this also partially negates the performance goal of the PR on large deployments.

adjudication.rationale: In `CleanAnnotations` MaxAge path, after `ids, err := r.fetchIDs(...)` succeeds, the code logs `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err)` (and similarly for count-based and tag cleanup). This is ERROR-level logging on the success path with `err` guaranteed to be nil, and it serializes the full `ids` slice, which can be as large as `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` (e.g., 32767 per the test). adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The MaxCount branch still uses fetchIDs with LimitOffset(batchSize, MaxCount) inside untilDoneOrCancelled, so each iteration deletes a batch of IDs that lie beyond the keep-count, meaning the callback can loop indefinitely re-selecting overlapping ranges if deletes don't shrink the qualifying set. If a batch's delete affects fewer rows than fetched (e.g., concurrent row re-creation or the under-delete path), the loop re-fetches the same offset window and can spin without progressing until context cancellation; the original single-statement loop's exit condition (zero affected rows) no longer maps cleanly to 'done' here.

adjudication.rationale: In the MaxCount branch, each untilDoneOrCancelled iteration re-runs `fetchIDs` with `LimitOffset(batchSize, cfg.MaxCount)` and then deletes exactly those IDs (`deleteByIDs`). Because the underlying qualifying set (rows beyond the keep-count) shrinks as those IDs are deleted, the next iteration’s OFFSET window will move to the next batch; it will not keep re-selecting the same IDs in a steady state. Termination is also reachable via `len(ids)==0` (which makes `deleteByIDs` return 0), so the loop does not depend on a fragile “affected==fetched” invariant. The claimed indefinite spin due to overlapping ranges is not supported by the diff’s logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The batch loop terminates on 'affected == 0' rather than on 'no IDs fetched', so when a fetched ID is concurrently deleted before the DELETE runs (race acknowledged in the comment), deleteByIDs returns affected < len(ids), and if an entire batch races the loop exits early having deleted only part of the eligible set while untilDoneOrCancelled reports success. A cleanup run silently under-deletes and returns nil error with a partial total; the comment says the next cycle compensates, but with the loop exiting on affected==0 the run's returned affectedAnnotations count understates the work, which the cleanup service records as the run's result.

The new batchWork implementations in CleanAnnotations/CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags fetch IDs (fetchIDs) then delete them (deleteByIDs) and return the DELETE’s RowsAffected. If concurrent activity removes the fetched rows before the DELETE executes, deleteByIDs can return 0 even though len(ids)>0, causing untilDoneOrCancelled to terminate early and skip subsequent batches that would still have eligible rows (because the next fetchIDs would return a different set). This leads to silent under-deletion and an understated totalAffected with nil error, matching the finding.
